title: NDFIP2 Suppresses Colorectal Cancer Metastasis Through DDX3X-Dependent R-Loop Remodeling and GNG13 Transcriptional Activation.
authors: Zhang, Enjian; Li, Yanfang; Shu, Jiaxin; Xu, Shang; Lv, Heng; Zhang, Chong; Zhang, Pengbo; Wu, Nai; Gong, Shuai; Zhang, Xiuzhong; Ren, Zeqiang; Zhang, Yi; Liu, Xin
abstract: Distant metastasis remains the leading cause of colorectal cancer (CRC) mortality, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Integrating RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiling and clinical validation, we identified NDFIP2 as significantly downregulated in metastatic CRC. Functionally, NDFIP2 loss drove epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), stemness, and metastasis via PI3K/AKT hyperactivation. Mechanistically, NDFIP2 serves as an adaptor recruiting the E3 ligase NEDD4 to induce K48-linked polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of DDX3X. Unrestrained DDX3X resolves R-loops at the GNG13 promoter and recruits the transcription factor CTCF, synergistically enhancing GNG13 transcription to amplify PI3K/AKT signaling. Targeting this vulnerability, we engineered a cell-permeable NDFIP2-derived iRGD-conjugated peptide (ND-iRGD). In vivo administration of this construct suppressed DDX3X/GNG13/PI3K/AKT signaling, thereby attenuating distant metastasis and prolonging murine survival. Collectively, NDFIP2 acts as a critical metastasis suppressor via the DDX3X/R-loop/GNG13 axis, presenting the ND-iRGD peptide as a promising translatable therapeutic strategy for metastatic CRC.

title: Exploring long noncoding RNAs as a molecular connection between immune response and autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition increasingly linked to immune dysregulation, with long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) emerging as potential regulators of both neural and immune processes. This study commenced by analyzing ten unique lncRNAs and integrated ASD whole-blood datasets using the online platform GTex to identify expression of lncRNAs in various tissues. Moreover, the platform Network Analyst was utilized to assess differentially expressed lncRNAs and associated transcriptomic networks. A total of 93 upregulated and 51 downregulated lncRNAs were identified in people with ASD with tissue specific enrichment observed for MSNP1AS and LNC01238 in immune related systems. The transcription factor CEBPA was shown to interact with the upregulated lncRNA MALAT1, which influenced immune cell differentiation, inflammation and cytokine signaling. Intriguingly CEBPA simultaneously interacted with downregulated lnc RNA MIR22HG. Comparatively, downregulated lncRNAs were associated with the transcription factors TEAD2, CEBPA, CTCF, E2F4, TFAP2C, HIF1A, ETS1, HNF4A, SNAPC4, STAT1, STAT2, TEAD2, FOXC1, BRCA1, AR, E2F4, EOMES, SPI1, DACH1, E2F1, TP63, HMAP1, KLF9, HDGF, and MAZ. Overall, the findings support a role for lncRNAs in ASD pathophysiology and immune dysregulation, pointing to their potential as biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets for future research.

title: PDS5A and TOP2B cooperate for chromatin recruitment via CTCF.
authors: Gonzalez-Buendia, Edgar; Ortabozkoyun, Havva; Reinberg, Danny
abstract: PDS5A, a cohesin regulatory subunit, and topoisomerase IIB (TOP2B), an enzyme resolving DNA topological problems, interact with CTCF and regulate transcription and genome organization. We ascertained that PDS5A and TOP2B are recruited to CTCF-bound chromatin cooperatively and that catalytically active TOP2B increases PDS5A occupancy genome wide. Notably, the amino-terminal 95 to 116 amino acids of CTCF interacts with PDS5A, giving rise to CTCF-PDS5A-TOP2B interaction in vitro and to PDS5A chromatin enrichment via active TOP2B in vivo. PDS5A-TOP2B function together in moderating the resultant gene expression and genome organization. Loss of CTCF (95 to 116 amino acids) led to dysregulated gene expression and mildly reduced chromatin loops. In gliomas, PDS5A and TOP2B expression levels vary, but correlate, contributing to distinctive gene expression patterns. Inducible PDS5A knockdown led to reduced TOP2B occupancy and altered gene expression. Furthermore, PDS5A mediated sensitivity to TOP2 cancer drugs in glioma cells. This functional interaction between PDS5A and TOP2B at CTCF boundaries expands upon the mechanisms affecting gene regulation through genome organization, with implications for glioma therapeutics.

title: CTCF contributes with alpha-satellite and satellite 2 expression in cancer cells: implications for centromeric chromatin organisation.
authors: Del Castillo Falconi, Victor M; Soto-Reyes Solis, Ernesto; Castillo-Gonzalez, Michelle; Ochoa, Carlos; Silva Diaz, Violeta Guadalupe; Delgado-Arzate, Ana Laura; Herrera, Luis A; Diaz-Chavez, Jose; Gonzalez-Barrios, Rodrigo
abstract: BACKGROUND: The centromeric and pericentromeric regions of chromosomes are essential for genome stability. Beyond their structural role, noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) transcribed from these regions have been implicated in kinetochore assembly. In cancer, reduced centromeric heterochromatin and deregulated ncRNA expression have been associated with chromosome instability. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: Centromeric and pericentromeric ncRNA expression was compared between the non-transformed WI-38 cell line and the colorectal cancer cell line HCT116. CTCF and H3K9me3 occupancy were evaluated by chromatin immunoprecipitation. Cells were treated with Trichostatin A (TSA), and CTCF function was assessed by pharmacological inhibition and shRNA-mediated depletion. RESULTS: Cancer cells exhibited elevated ncRNA levels, accompanied by reduced H3K9me3 enrichment and differential CTCF occupancy. Functional inactivation or depletion of CTCF markedly decreased ncRNA transcription, supporting a role for CTCF in regulating centromeric and pericentromeric ncRNAs. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support an association between chromatin state, CTCF occupancy, and ncRNA transcription at centromeric regions, and provide insight into epigenetic patterns associated with genome stability in cancer cells. Our results further suggest that centromeric chromatin operates within constrained transcriptional states compatible with chromosome stability.

title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin.
authors: Debek, Sonia; Meydan, Cem; Chin, Christopher R; Yu, Jiali; Durmaz, Ceyda; Tsialta, Ioanna; Pelzer, Benedikt; Maurer, Constance; Ou, Arnold; Laguillo-Diego, Alejandra; Scourzic, Laurianne; Tumuluru, Sravya; Teater, Matt; Wu, Rui; Darsow, Brian; Rivas, Martin A; Marin-Rubio, Jose Luis; Stadtfeld, Matthias; Apostolou, Effie; Mason, Christopher E; Elenitoba-Johnson, Kojo S J; Risca, Viviana I; Melnick, Ari; Barisic, Darko
abstract: The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding(1,2). Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types(3). However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF-cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer-promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

title: Layered regulation of plant 3D chromatin architecture by histone marks, transcription factors and cohesin‑mediated loops.
authors: Su, Zezhao; Wang, Zhidan; Latrasse, David; Liu, Chang; Benhamed, Moussa
abstract: The three-dimensional (3D) organization of the genome has emerged as a central layer of gene regulation in eukaryotes. In plants, chromatin architecture displays both conserved features and lineage-specific characteristics, reflecting differences in genome composition, epigenetic landscapes and regulatory strategies. Recent evolutionary analyses suggest that plants preferentially adopt a chromosome-scale "global folding" strategy distinct from the compartmentalized architecture observed in animals, which raises an important question: how is regulatory information coordinated in plants in the absence of canonical architectural proteins such as CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) and strong compartmental domains? Here, we discuss evidence supporting a model in which plant 3D genome organization arises from the interplay between three major regulatory layers: chromatin states defined by histone modifications, transcription factor-mediated regulatory interactions, and cohesin-dependent chromatin extrusion. We further propose that these mechanisms operate within a global folding framework that balances structural stability with regulatory plasticity.

title: An extensible deep learning framework for multi-type chromatin interaction prediction through hierarchical adaptation strategies.
authors: Wang, Shuaibin; Chen, Tong; Liu, Weixu; Zheng, Xuejie; Yang, Zhongxin; Liang, Zhen; Shen, Yin
abstract: Three-dimensional chromatin interactions play essential roles in gene regulation, yet computational prediction of diverse interaction types remains largely dependent on specialized, single-task models. Here, we present UniLoopNet, a multi-task deep learning framework that predicts multiple types of chromatin interactions including enhancer-promoter interactions, enhancer-enhancer interactions, CTCF-mediated loops, and stripe-associated interactions from DNA sequences. UniLoopNet employs a shared encoder-decoder architecture with hierarchical adaptation strategies, integrating multi-task, transfer, and continual learning based on task semantic similarity. Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple cell lines demonstrates that UniLoopNet outperforms existing specialized and multi-task approaches, with AUROCs exceeding 0.90 in most tasks. Under stringent evaluation settings, including chromosome-matched, distance-matched, realistic imbalanced, and locus-disjoint tests, AUROCs range from 0.8934 to 0.9366. In the realistic 1:5 class-imbalance setting, the AUPRCs for enhancer-promoter and enhancer-enhancer interaction prediction are 0.7956 and 0.6935, respectively. Cross-cell-line transfer experiments further show that applying UniLoopNet to another cell line requires adaptation by supervised fine-tuning on target-cell-line data, after which performance is comparable to that of within-cell-line training. Notably, the framework exhibits data efficiency in experiments with substantially reduced training data. Interpretability analyses reveal that the learned sequence features are associated with known transcription factor binding sites and uncover differential regulatory effects of disease-associated variants. UniLoopNet provides a versatile and data-efficient framework for sequence-based prediction and interpretation of diverse 3D genome interactions, complementing existing sequence-to-map approaches while improving the understanding of sequence-encoded regulatory potential.

title: How Does HTLV-1 Persist in the Host?
abstract: HTLV-1 resists clearance from its host by the strong HTLV-1-specific immune response and by drugs. The tactics and strategies by which it does so illustrate the exquisite adaptation to the host that HTLV-1 has made in its tens of thousands of years of stable co-existence with humans. This adaptation contrasts strongly with the biology of HIV-1, which has established widespread infection in humans for only around a century. The mode of persistence of HTLV-1 makes it less pathogenic than HIV-1, despite causing serious malignant and inflammatory diseases in a proportion of people with the virus, but at the same time makes HTLV-1 harder to treat and eradicate. In this article I outline the different means that HTLV-1 has evolved to persist in the host.

title: DNA-Encoded Binding Affinity Shapes Robust CTCF Occupancy Across Cellular Contexts.
authors: Yin, Zihang; Wang, Yefan; Zhang, Zhiyu; Wang, Wuming; Guo, Ya
abstract: CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) is an architectural protein that organizes 3D genome architecture by binding to tens of thousands of genomic loci in a typical human cell type. Although DNA-binding affinity contributes to CTCF occupancy in vivo, the principles distinguishing robust from context-dependent occupancy remain incompletely understood. Here, we integrated quantitative measurements of CTCF-DNA binding affinity with genome-wide occupancy profiles. Using synthetic tandem arrays of CTCF sites with defined affinity levels, we experimentally tested whether DNA-encoded affinity establishes a predictable hierarchy of CTCF occupancy in vivo. We identified two CTCF-DNA binding affinity thresholds defining three distinct CTCF occupancy regimes. High-affinity sites were more frequently and consistently occupied across diverse cellular contexts and chromatin environments, whereas intermediate- and low-affinity sites showed greater context dependence. Synthetic arrays further revealed a reproducible occupancy hierarchy that was maintained across different motif arrangements. High-affinity sites were preferentially associated with strong chromatin loops and TAD boundaries, and flanking CTCF motifs that contribute to binding affinity were enriched at strong loop anchors. Together, these findings establish a quantitative framework in which CTCF-DNA binding affinity links sequence-encoded binding properties to the robustness and context dependence of CTCF occupancy and to features of CTCF-mediated 3D genome organization.

title: Genome-Wide Chromatin Structure Changes During Caste Differentiation in Honeybees.
authors: Zhang, Xinru; Lu, Hanbing; Qu, Xinying; Xin, Lingjun; Wang, Rongshen; Liang, Chongbo; Liu, Xiaopeng; Chen, Xiao
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture is an important transcription regulator which is linked to gene expression regulation and correct developmental programs, yet little is known that the 3D chromatin architecture within honeybees and how it influences gene expression and methylation in caste differentiation. Here, we report that larvae at 96 h after hatching (L5) contain the highest number of known caste differentiation genes, and that constitutes the critical window determining the final phenotypic outcomes. We also show that DNA methylation pattern is conserved and gene body methylation is thought to contribute to phenotypic plasticity. Then, we determine the 3D organization of honey bee chromosomes at 5 kb resolution. Although almost 87% regions remained in the same compartments, TAD boundary insulation increased during larvae development, especially in worker larvae at 96 h after hatching (WL5). The insulator protein, CP190, CTCF-L and vtd/Rad21 appear to be indispensable in defining these topologically associating domain boundaries. Furthermore, Mrjp1, a member of the MRJP/yellow family, is also involved in regulating larval development. These results provide key insights into caste differentiation and establish a fundamental dataset for the future in-depth characterization of epigenetic features.

title: A CTCF-LDHB axis converts nuclear lactate availability into an H3K18 acylation switch that directs alternative splicing in hypoxic breast cancer
authors: Kakani P; Brahma A; Jithin B; Peter RM; Panda A; Bansal A; Kumar OP; Niyati K; Sahu A; Samaiya A; Shukla S
abstract: Lactate accumulating in hypoxic tumours lactylates histones, coupling metabolic state to chromatin. Why it differs between tumours of comparable glycolytic rate has remained unresolved. Here we show that nuclear, rather than total intracellular, lactate availability determines histone H3K18 lactylation in breast cancer, and that CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) and lactate dehydrogenase B ( LDHB ) jointly set it. CTCF sustains glycolytic gene expression under hypoxia and drives LDHB in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), whereas a CTCF-ERα complex represses LDHB in non-TNBC. LDHB consumes lactate favouring H3K18 acetylation; where LDHB is low, CTCF-dependent MCT1 delivers lactate into the nucleus and sustains lactylation. At a CTCF site downstream of TACC3 exon 3, an invariant polymerase II pause couples kinetic and adaptor control of splicing, with the mark deciding the outcome: H3K18la recruits SMARCA4 and hnRNPA1 to skip the exon, generating an isoform that drives EMT, whereas H3K18ac recruits TRIM33 and SRSF10 to include it, generating one that confers stemness. Inhibiting LDHB restores exon skipping and suppresses tumour growth in vivo. Nuclear lactate availability therefore acts as a metabolic switch that converts hypoxic stress into subtype-specific splicing decisions and identifies LDHB as a tractable target in TNBC.

title: Engineered Tn5 Variants Enhance CUT&Tag Fidelity for Transcription Factors
authors: Piper L; Baird E; Ashbaugh HJ; Pentecost OA; Nowinski SM; Janssens DH
abstract: The CUT&Tag method performs exceptionally well for profiling histone modifications, but mapping sequence-specific transcription factors (TFs) is complicated by intrinsic Tn5 activity at accessible DNA, and the high-salt washes used to suppress this activity can destabilize TF-chromatin interactions. We engineered the Tn5 DNA-binding channel to attenuate target-DNA engagement by replacing individual positively charged amino acids with neutral amino acids. We identified a “Goldilocks” variant (K160A) with intermediate attenuation that improved recovery of GATA2 motif-containing sites under low-salt CUT&Tag and KCl-based DynaTag conditions. A second variant (K249A) had improved performance for profiling CTCF over less accessible sites characterized by sharply focused short-fragment enrichment. By comparing the K160A and K249A variants, this TF-CUT&Tag assay provides a physical readout of the local chromatin environment at TF binding sites. Applying K160A TF-CUT&Tag to pluripotency-associated TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells increased recovery across their genomic binding landscapes while preserving factor-specific motif architectures. During skeletal muscle differentiation, TF-CUT&Tag improved recovery of MyoG and Pax7 occupancy relative to standard CUT&Tag, revealing strongly motif-enriched MyoG binding and a shift in Pax7 binding from CpG-rich promoters in progenitors toward Pax7 motif-enriched sites during differentiation. Together, these results show that TF-CUT&Tag captures distinct modes of TF– chromatin interaction, including motif-directed binding sites and more salt-sensitive sites that may depend on lower-affinity DNA recognition or protein–protein interactions and are difficult to predict from DNA sequence alone.

title: Histone modifications define distinct nucleosome positions in cell-free DNA
authors: Ou Y; Gulati GS; Tyndall CF; Pandey M; Seo J; Zhang Z; Jin Z; Lee GG; Nawfal R; Hoggood TA; Shahbazi SD; Ludwig J; Zhang Z; Ibrahim E; Nafeh G; Berchuck JE; Sowalsky AG; Karzai F; Freedman ML; Takeda DY; Baca SC
abstract:
ABSTRACT

Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentation patterns reflect nucleosome positioning. We asked whether variation in nucleosome positions in cfDNA can reveal chromatin states and associated histone modifications. Using cell-free chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (cfChIP-seq) in plasma from patients with prostate cancer, we identified 35,120 modification-associated positions (MAPs), loci where nucleosomes bearing active (H3K4me2) and repressive (H3K9me3) histone marks occupy reproducibly offset positions. These offsets recurred across histone marks, an independent cfChIP-seq cohort, and nuclease-digested chromatin from cell lines. MAPs were enriched in transcribed genes but depleted near transcription start sites and CTCF-binding sites where nucleosome positioning is constrained. Across 2,535 cfDNA sequencing datasets, nucleosome protection at a subset of MAPs correlated with tumor fraction (TF), reflecting differences in histone modification status between cancer-derived and non-malignant chromatin. In targeted sequencing panels, a 50-MAP model using fragments from < 0.001% of the genome distinguished samples with tumor fractions ≥3% vs 0% (AUCs = 0.91-0.96 across prostate, breast, and lung cancers) and outperformed a state-of-the-art fragmentomics-based tumor fraction predictor. MAP-derived estimates correlated with reference TFs ( r = 0.89) and longitudinal changes in TF ( r = 0.91). MAP protection at ASCL1 binding sites identified neuroendocrine transformation of prostate cancer from cfDNA. These findings establish histone-modification-associated nucleosome positioning as a mutation-independent readout of tumor fraction and cancer state from routine cfDNA sequencing.

title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility
authors: Lee J; Zhang K; Shurberg E; Ramani VS; Pollard KS
abstract: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis-regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

title: Does a map-level insulation constraint improve sequence-based prediction of 3D genome folding? A Stage 1 Registered Report with a reverse-complement-equivariant state-space model (HiFold-Mamba)
abstract:
Background:

Sequence-to-contact-map models are trained with pixel-wise losses, although the features of interest (insulation, domain boundaries, loops) are summaries of the map. Insulationbased losses help Hi-C resolution enhancement. No pre-specified test has asked whether they improve sequence-based prediction, judged against annotations independent of the training data. Proposed study. HiFold-Mamba predicts 448 × 448 maps at 2,048 bp from 1,048,576 bp of DNA on the DNALongBench contact-map task. Every component is reverse-complement-equivariant: convolutional tower, bidirectional Mamba blocks, multi-scale mixer and symmetric pairwise head. We pre-register three hypotheses: » H1: it exceeds each of three trained baselines (reproduced Akita, a parameter-matched Transformer and a parameter-matched CNN) by ≥0.01 stratum-adjusted correlation (SCC). » H2: an insulation and boundary loss, computed from the predicted map with the operator used on the observed map, improves boundary AUROC and loop AP against independent 4DN boundary calls and ENCODE CTCF ChIA-PET loops, at equal training steps and without loss of SCC. » H3: pretraining plus few-shot adaptation beats training from scratch on four held-out cell lines.Tests use a paired bootstrap over 237 one-megabase test blocks (one-sided α = 0.025). Pilot data. » Verification. The benchmark target, the window coordinates and the networks equivariance were verified. » Locus-shared reference. Copying other cell lines measured maps at the same locus matches published Akita on the benchmarks SCC (0.227 vs. 0.230). » SCC weightings. Two weightings in common use weight distance strata in opposite directions and agree only moderately (ρ = 0.54). » Comparison rule. In simulations calibrated on the pilot data, a per-block-best comparison against several baselines has no power. We therefore test against each baseline, which gives ≥ 90 % power at a true gain of 0.02 when between-model correlation is ≥ 0.95. » H2 positive control. On validation windows, observed maps recover the independent boundaries (AUROC 0.61 − 0.91) and loops (0.86 − 0.90). This fixed the insulation window and showed that these annotations are largely shared across cell types.
